amt.behoerden.pir.hru: Naturalisations are processed centrally in Pirna – also for Freital. Make an appointment in advance. You only sign the application at the appointment in front of the case officer. A detailed CV in German written as continuous text (NOT as a table) is required. dtz.info: The German Test for Immigrants (DTZ) tests levels A2 and B1. For naturalisation you need B1 in all parts. Parts: listening (approx. 25 min), reading (45 min), writing (30 min), speaking (approx. 16 min, with a partner). Other B1 certificates are also accepted (e.g. Goethe, telc, ÖSD) – ask your authority.

info.check.aufenthalt: How long have you been living lawfully and habitually in Germany?
info.check.aufenthalt.o.1: 3–5 years and married to a German (for at least 2 years)
info.check.aufenthalt.o.2: 3–5 years, not married to a German
info.check.aufenthalt.o.2.hru: Naturalisation after 3 years for special integration achievements was abolished on 30.10.2025. You usually need 5 years.
info.check.aufenthalt.o.3.hru: Use the time for German and the test – then you will be ready as soon as the period is up.
info.check.deutsch.o.0: I have a B1 certificate (or higher) or a German school-leaving certificate
info.check.deutsch.o.1.hru: The German course in this app will take you to B1.
info.check.deutsch.o.2.hru: Start with lesson A1.1 – 20 minutes a day is enough for a good start.
info.check.fdgo: Can you commit to the free democratic basic order – including Germany's historical responsibility (protecting Jewish life) and equal rights for men and women?
info.check.fdgo.o.1: I am not sure what this means
info.check.fdgo.o.1.hru: The test questions on "Politics in a democracy" and "History and responsibility" explain it. The authority will also read the declaration to you.
info.check.geld: How do you support yourself (and your family)?
info.check.geld.o.1: I receive supplementary Bürgergeld or social assistance
info.check.geld.o.1.hru: In principle, you must be able to support yourself without these benefits. There are narrow exceptions (e.g. full-time work for 20 of the last 24 months, former guest/contract workers). Check with the authority.
info.check.geld.o.2: Studies/vocational training financed by BAföG or family
info.check.geld.o.2.hru: BAföG does not count as social assistance. Check your individual case.
info.check.pass: Is your identity established (valid passport, birth certificate)?
info.check.pass.o.0: Yes, I have my passport and certificates
info.check.pass.o.1.hru: Naturalisation is not possible without an established identity. But if documents genuinely cannot be obtained, there are other ways of proving it – discuss this with the authority in advance.
info.check.straf: Have you been convicted of a criminal offence?
info.check.straf.o.1: Yes, only a minor penalty (e.g. a fine of up to 90 daily rates)
info.check.straf.o.1.hru: Minor penalties are often disregarded – except where the motives were antisemitic, racist or otherwise inhumane. Check with the authority.
info.check.straf.o.2.hru: This may rule out naturalisation. Get individual advice (e.g. from a migration advice service).
info.check.test.o.0: Passed (at least 17 out of 33) or German school-leaving certificate
info.check.test.o.1.hru: Practise with the trainer and take practice exams until you reliably score more than 25.
info.check.titel: What residence status do you have?
info.check.titel.o.0: Settlement permit, EU long-term residence or EU/EEA/Swiss citizen
info.check.titel.o.1: Temporary residence permit for work/family, EU Blue Card, recognised refugee
info.check.titel.o.1.hru: Many temporary residence permits qualify if they are intended for a long stay. Check with the authority.
info.check.titel.o.2: Temporary protection (§ 24, e.g. Ukraine), studies/vocational training
info.check.titel.o.2.hru: With these residence permits there is usually no right to naturalisation. Switching to another permit (e.g. for work) may open the way – get advice.
info.check.titel.o.3: Toleration (Duldung) or permission to remain during the asylum procedure (Aufenthaltsgestattung)
info.check.titel.o.3.hru: Naturalisation is not possible with a Duldung or Gestattung.

info.gespraech.bekenntnis.1: Before naturalisation you sign a declaration. In it you commit to the free democratic basic order of the Basic Law: human dignity, democracy, the rule of law, equal rights. You declare that you do not support any activities against the constitution. Since 2024 this has also included commitment to Germany's special historical responsibility – in particular the protection of Jewish life – and to the peaceful coexistence of nations. When the certificate is handed over, you make a solemn declaration. Read the declaration calmly beforehand and ask if there is anything you do not understand.
info.gespraech.fragen.0.aru: I have lived in Germany for many years. My family and my work are here. I would also like to be able to vote and have a say.
info.gespraech.fragen.0.qru: Why would you like German citizenship?
info.gespraech.fragen.1.aru: I have lived in Germany since 2019, and here in Freital since 2021.
info.gespraech.fragen.1.qru: Since when have you lived in Germany?
info.gespraech.fragen.2.aru: I work full time as a qualified care worker in a care home for the elderly in Pirna.
info.gespraech.fragen.3.aru: First I attended an integration course. Then I kept learning at work and with an app. In March I passed the B1 exam.
info.gespraech.fragen.4.aru: For me, democracy means that the people decide in free elections and that everyone may say what they think.
info.gespraech.fragen.4.qru: What does democracy mean to you?
info.gespraech.fragen.5.aru: Men and women have the same rights – in the family, at work and before the law. For example, both have an equal say about money and children.
info.gespraech.fragen.5.qru: What does equal rights for men and women mean?
info.gespraech.fragen.6.aru: Because of the crimes of the National Socialists, above all the Holocaust. That is why Germany must give special protection to Jewish life, and antisemitism has no place here.
info.gespraech.fragen.6.qru: Why does Germany have a special responsibility for Jewish life?
info.gespraech.fragen.7.aru: No, everything has stayed the same. / Yes, I changed jobs in July. I have brought my new employment contract.
info.gespraech.fragen.7.qru: Have you changed your address or your job since you applied?
info.gespraech.fragen.8.aru: No, I have never been convicted.
info.gespraech.fragen.8.qru: Have you been convicted in Germany or abroad?
info.gespraech.fragen.9.aru: Yes: roughly how long does processing take, and do I need to hand in anything else?
info.gespraech.intro.1: At the appointment the authority checks your documents and talks to you briefly – often also to hear your German. It is not a test you can fail. Answer calmly in simple, complete sentences.

info.steps.s1.dru: Use the requirements check in this app to see honestly where you stand. The authority also gives free, non-binding advice.
info.steps.s2.dru: Work through the A1 to B1 course in the app, then take a recognised B1 exam (e.g. DTZ, Goethe, telc, ÖSD).
info.steps.s3.dru: Learn all 310 questions (300 general + 10 on Saxony), take practice exams, then register at an adult education centre (VHS); fee 25 €.
info.steps.s4.dru: Certificates from your country of origin and certified translations often take months. Start early!
info.steps.s5.dru: The district office (Landratsamt) of your district is responsible, or the city administration in Chemnitz, Dresden and Leipzig. Many authorities first check the requirements by email and then send the forms.
info.steps.s6.dru: Submit the application in writing with all the evidence (some authorities also accept it online). From the age of 16 you apply yourself.
info.steps.s7.dru: Processing often takes a year or longer (the Mittelsachsen district says 12–15 months). Tell the authority immediately about a move, a change of job or new children.
info.steps.s8.dru: Naturalisation takes effect when you receive the naturalisation certificate in person. At this point you make a solemn declaration of commitment to the free democratic basic order. Fee: 255 € per adult.
info.steps.s9.dru: Apply for an ID card and passport at the citizens' office. Check whether your country of origin requires you to report a second citizenship. From now on you may vote in all elections.

info.waehlen.intro.1: After naturalisation you may take part in all elections in Germany. This is how it works in Saxony.
info.waehlen.punkte.0.2: Who can vote? German citizens aged 18 and over – in federal, state and local elections in Saxony. In the European election from 16.
info.waehlen.punkte.1.2: Do I have to register? No. Anyone registered at the residents' registration office is automatically on the electoral roll.
info.waehlen.punkte.2.2: Polling card: a few weeks before the election you receive a letter from the municipality with the date, the polling station and the application for a postal vote. If no letter arrives, ask the municipality.
info.waehlen.punkte.3.2: At the polling station: take your polling card and ID. Mark your crosses in the booth, fold the ballot paper and put it in the ballot box. Voting is secret – nobody may watch.
info.waehlen.punkte.4.2: Postal vote: apply with the polling card or online at your municipality. The documents arrive by post. Send off the red ballot envelope in good time – it must arrive by 6 pm on election day.
info.waehlen.punkte.5.2: Federal election: two votes – the first vote for a person from your constituency, the second vote for a party. The second vote decides the seats.
info.waehlen.punkte.6.2: Saxon state election: also two votes – a direct vote for a person and a list vote for a party. Elections are held every five years.
info.waehlen.punkte.7.2: Local elections in Saxony: you have three votes each for the municipal or town council and the district council. You may give them all to one person (cumulating) or spread them over people on different lists (panachage).
info.waehlen.punkte.8.2: Become an election helper: many municipalities look for volunteer election helpers and pay a small allowance. A good opportunity to get to know people.
k.a1-1.dia.0.2: Good afternoon! My name is Müller. What is your name?
k.a1-1.dia.1.2: Good afternoon! My name is Irina Smirnova.
k.a1-1.dia.2.2: Where are you from, Ms Smirnova?
k.a1-1.dia.3.2: I am from Kazakhstan. I live in Dresden now.
k.a1-1.gr: The verbs sein (to be) and heißen (to be called), personal pronouns
k.a1-1.gr.ex.3.1: Where are you from? – I am from Ukraine.
k.a1-1.gr.rde: In a German statement the verb is in position 2. "sein" is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. "Sie" with a capital S is the polite form of "you" – at public offices always use "Sie".
k.a1-10.dia.0.2: Hello, I would like to register. I have moved.
k.a1-10.dia.1.2: Do you have your passport and the landlord's confirmation?
k.a1-10.dia.3.2: Thank you. Please also fill in the form and sign at the bottom.
k.a1-10.gr.ex.1.1: I was born on 5 June 1988 in Minsk.
k.a1-10.gr.rde: Forms always ask for the same details. Dates: am 3. Mai = am dritten Mai (on the third of May); geboren am 12.04.1990 = am zwölften vierten neunzehnhundertneunzig. Unterschrift = signature (your name written by hand).
k.a1-2.dia.3.2: Kowalenko. K – O – W – A – L – E – N – K – O.
k.a1-2.gr.rde: From 21 onwards, German numbers are said "backwards": 21 = einundzwanzig (one-and-twenty). At public offices you often have to spell your name: A as in Anton, B as in Berta …
k.a1-3.dia.1.2: Yes. My husband's name is Sergej. We have a daughter.
k.a1-3.dia.3.2: She is eight. She goes to school.
k.a1-3.gr.ex.1.1: My son is five years old.
k.a1-3.gr.ex.2.1: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
k.a1-3.gr.ex.3.1: I am married and have two children.
k.a1-3.gr.rde: German nouns have a gender: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter). Possessive articles follow it: mein Vater (der), meine Mutter (die), mein Kind (das), meine Kinder (plural). Learn every noun with its article!
k.a1-4.dia.1.2: I would like a loaf of bread and 200 grams of cheese, please.
k.a1-4.dia.3.2: No, thank you. How much is that?
k.a1-4.gr.ex.1.1: I am buying milk and a loaf of bread.
k.a1-4.gr.ex.3.1: How much is that? – That is 2.50 euros.
k.a1-4.gr.rde: After "haben", "kaufen" and "möchten" the accusative is used. Only masculine articles change: der → den, ein → einen. Nouns are negated with "kein": Ich habe keinen Hunger (I am not hungry).
k.a1-5.dia.0.2: What is your new flat like?
k.a1-5.dia.1.2: It's lovely! It has two rooms, a kitchen and a balcony.
k.a1-5.dia.3.2: No, not very. The rent is 550 euros including heating.
k.a1-5.gr: Adjectives after sein, negation with nicht
k.a1-5.gr.ex.1.1: The kitchen is small but bright.
k.a1-5.gr.ex.3.1: We are looking for a flat in Pirna.
k.a1-5.gr.rde: After "sein" the adjective does not change: Die Wohnung ist groß (The flat is big). Verbs and adjectives are negated with "nicht": Die Wohnung ist nicht teuer. Nouns with "kein".
k.a1-6.dia.1.2: At six. At half past seven I take the children to nursery.
k.a1-6.dia.3.2: Then I start work at eight.
k.a1-6.gr.ex.0.1: I get up at half past six.
k.a1-6.gr.ex.2.1: In the evening I phone my mother.
k.a1-6.gr.ex.3.1: What time is it? – It is a quarter past ten.
k.a1-6.gr.rde: With separable verbs the prefix goes to the end of the sentence: aufstehen → Ich stehe um 6 Uhr auf (I get up at 6). Others: einkaufen, anrufen, fernsehen. Official time: 14:30 = vierzehn Uhr dreißig; informal: halb drei (half past two).
k.a1-7.dia.0.2: Excuse me, how do I get to the town hall?
k.a1-7.dia.1.2: Go straight ahead here as far as the traffic lights. Then right.
k.a1-7.dia.3.2: No, only five minutes on foot.
k.a1-7.gr: Prepositions with the dative: mit, zu, bei, von, aus, nach
k.a1-7.gr.ex.0.1: How do I get to the station?
k.a1-7.gr.ex.1.1: Go straight ahead and then left.
k.a1-7.gr.ex.2.1: I am taking the S-Bahn (suburban train) to Dresden.
k.a1-7.gr.ex.3.1: The district office is next to the post office.
k.a1-7.gr.rde: After mit, zu, bei, von, aus, nach and seit, the dative always follows: der → dem, das → dem, die → der. Ich fahre mit dem Bus (I go by bus). Ich gehe zum (= zu dem) Arzt (I go to the doctor). Zur (= zu der) Post (to the post office).
k.a1-8.dia.1.2: Good morning, I have a temperature and a sore throat. Can I come today?
k.a1-8.dia.2.2: Yes, come at eleven o'clock. Bring your health insurance card.
k.a1-8.dia.3.2: Thank you very much. I also need a sick note for my employer.
k.a1-8.gr: Modal verbs können, müssen, dürfen; imperative (Sie)
k.a1-8.gr.ex.3.1: Please bring your health insurance card.
k.a1-8.gr.rde: Modal verb in position 2, infinitive at the end: Ich muss zum Arzt gehen (I have to go to the doctor). Forms: ich kann/muss/darf, du kannst/musst/darfst. Polite instruction: Nehmen Sie die Tabletten dreimal täglich (Take the tablets three times a day).

k.a1-9.gr: W-questions and yes/no questions, introduction to the Perfekt
k.a1-9.gr.ex.0.1: What is your job? – I am a nurse.
k.a1-9.gr.ex.1.1: I work full time for a company in Freital.
k.a1-9.gr.ex.2.1: Do you have an employment contract?

k.a1-9.gr.rde: W-question: question word in position 1 (Was machen Sie beruflich? – What do you do for a living?). Yes/no question: verb in position 1 (Arbeiten Sie hier? – Do you work here?). We usually talk about the past using the Perfekt: Ich habe in Kiew als Lehrerin gearbeitet (I worked as a teacher in Kyiv).
k.a2-1.dia.0.2: Since when have you lived in Germany?
k.a2-1.dia.1.2: For six years. I came in 2020.

k.a2-1.gr.ex.3.1: Have you already taken the test?
k.a2-1.gr.rde: Perfekt = haben/sein (position 2) + past participle (at the end). Regular: ge…t (gemacht, gearbeitet). Irregular: ge…en (gefahren, gegessen). Verbs of movement and change form the Perfekt with "sein": Ich bin nach Deutschland gekommen (I came to Germany). Ich bin umgezogen (I moved house).

k.a2-10.gr: Overview of word order: main clause, subordinate clause, verb bracket
k.a2-10.gr.ex.0.1: When I have time, I learn German.
k.a2-10.gr.ex.1.1: Yesterday I studied for a long time.
k.a2-10.gr.ex.2.1: Tomorrow I have to get up early.
k.a2-10.gr.ex.3.1: Do you know when the exam starts?
k.a2-10.gr.rde: Main clause: verb in position 2. Yes/no question: verb in position 1. Verb bracket: auxiliary/modal verb in position 2, participle/infinitive/prefix at the end. Subordinate clause (weil, dass, wenn, ob): conjugated verb at the end. If the subordinate clause comes first, the verb follows immediately: Wenn ich Zeit habe, lerne ich.
k.a2-2.dia.0.2: Good morning, this is Mrs Petrenko. My son Max is in class 2b.
k.a2-2.dia.2.2: Max cannot come today because he is ill.
k.a2-2.dia.3.2: Get well soon! Please give him a written absence note tomorrow.
k.a2-2.gr: Subordinate clauses with weil and dass
k.a2-2.gr.ex.0.1: My son cannot come today because he has a temperature.
k.a2-2.gr.ex.1.1: The teacher says there is a parents' evening tomorrow.
k.a2-2.gr.ex.2.1: We are looking for a nursery place.
k.a2-2.gr.ex.3.1: Compulsory schooling starts at the age of six.
k.a2-2.gr.rde: In a subordinate clause the conjugated verb goes to the end: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil mein Kind krank ist (I am staying at home because my child is ill). Ich weiß, dass die Schule um 8 Uhr beginnt (I know that school starts at 8). Put a comma before "weil" and "dass".

k.a2-3.gr: Two-way prepositions (in, an, auf …): Where? / Where to?
k.a2-3.gr.ex.0.1: The heating in the bathroom isn't working.
k.a2-3.gr.ex.1.1: I put the rubbish outside the door.
k.a2-3.gr.ex.2.1: The key is on the table.
k.a2-3.gr.rde: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen: "Where?" → dative (Das Bild hängt an der Wand – The picture hangs on the wall). "Where to?" → accusative (Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand – I hang the picture on the wall).

k.a2-4.gr.ex.0.1: I would like an appointment about naturalisation.

k.a2-4.gr.rde: Asking politely: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? (Could you help me, please?) Ich hätte gern einen Termin (I would like an appointment). Würden Sie mir das bitte erklären? (Would you explain that to me, please?) Formal letter: greeting "Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren," – closing "Mit freundlichen Grüßen".

k.a2-5.gr.rde: Reflexive verbs have a reflexive pronoun: sich anmelden, sich fühlen, sich ausruhen. ich → mich, du → dich, er/sie → sich, wir → uns, ihr → euch, sie/Sie → sich. Ich fühle mich nicht gut (I don't feel well).

k.a2-6.gr.rde: Comparative: -er (schnell → schneller), often with an umlaut (alt → älter). Comparison: als (Teilzeit ist flexibler als Vollzeit – part time is more flexible than full time). Superlative: am …sten (am schnellsten). Irregular: gut – besser – am besten, viel – mehr – am meisten, gern – lieber – am liebsten.

k.a2-7.gr: Verbs with prepositions; adjective endings after the definite article
k.a2-7.gr.ex.1.1: We are looking forward to the town festival.
k.a2-7.gr.ex.2.1: My son is in the sports club.
k.a2-7.gr.ex.3.1: On 3 October we celebrate the Day of German Unity.
k.a2-7.gr.rde: Many verbs have a fixed preposition: sich interessieren für (to be interested in), sich freuen auf/über (to look forward to / be happy about), teilnehmen an (to take part in), warten auf (to wait for). Adjectives after der/die/das: der neue Verein, die neue Nachbarin – in the plural and in most dative/accusative forms -en: mit dem neuen Freund.

k.a2-8.gr: Subordinate clauses with wenn, ob and question words (indirect questions)
k.a2-8.gr.ex.0.1: I would like to open a current account.
k.a2-8.gr.ex.1.1: If the bill is wrong, I'll phone.
k.a2-8.gr.ex.2.1: Do you know whether I can cancel the contract immediately?
k.a2-8.gr.ex.3.1: Read the contract carefully before you sign.
k.a2-8.gr.rde: Condition: Wenn Sie den Vertrag kündigen wollen, müssen Sie schriftlich kündigen (If you want to cancel the contract, you must do so in writing). Indirect question: Können Sie mir sagen, ob das Konto kostenlos ist? (…whether the account is free?) Ich möchte wissen, wie viel das kostet. The verb always goes at the end.

k.a2-9.gr: Giving your opinion; simple past of sein, haben and modal verbs
k.a2-9.gr.ex.0.1: I think news on the radio is good for learning.
k.a2-9.gr.ex.1.1: Yesterday I was tired, I couldn't study.

k.a2-9.gr.rde: Opinion: Ich finde, dass … (I think that …) / Meiner Meinung nach … (In my opinion …) / Ich glaube, … Agreeing: Da hast du recht (You're right there). Disagreeing: Das sehe ich anders (I see it differently). Simple past: war, hatte, konnte, musste, wollte – these forms are also used in speech.

k.b1-1.gr: Simple past in texts, time clauses with als, nachdem, bevor
k.b1-1.gr.ex.0.1: I was born on 4 March 1990 in Kharkiv.
k.b1-1.gr.ex.1.1: From 1996 to 2007 I attended School No. 12.
k.b1-1.gr.ex.2.1: After I had completed my degree, I worked as an engineer.
k.b1-1.gr.rde: In written texts (e.g. a detailed CV) you narrate in the simple past (Präteritum): ich ging, ich arbeitete, ich zog um. "als" for one-off events in the past: Als ich 18 war, begann ich zu studieren (When I was 18, I started university). "nachdem" + past perfect: Nachdem ich die Schule beendet hatte, machte ich eine Ausbildung (After I had finished school, I did vocational training).

k.b1-10.gr: Talking about values, giving reasons, Konjunktiv II for wishes
k.b1-10.gr.ex.0.1: I have lived here for eight years; Germany has become my home.
k.b1-10.gr.ex.1.1: I want to have a say, because my family lives here.
k.b1-10.gr.ex.2.1: I commit to the free democratic basic order.
k.b1-10.gr.ex.3.1: For me, democracy means that everyone may say what they think freely.
k.b1-10.gr.rde: At the appointment you will be asked why you want to become German, and you will make a declaration of commitment to the free democratic basic order. Give reasons with weil, denn, deshalb. Wishes: Ich würde gern wählen (I would like to vote). Ich möchte, dass meine Kinder hier sicher aufwachsen (I want my children to grow up safely here).

k.b1-2.gr: Passive in the present and simple past
k.b1-2.gr.ex.0.1: In Germany elections are free, equal and secret.
k.b1-2.gr.ex.1.1: Laws are passed by the Bundestag.
k.b1-2.gr.ex.2.1: The Basic Law was adopted in 1949.
k.b1-2.gr.ex.3.1: The Saxon Landtag is elected every five years.
k.b1-2.gr.rde: Passive = werden + past participle. The action matters, not the person: Der Bundestag wird alle vier Jahre gewählt (The Bundestag is elected every four years). Die Bundesrepublik wurde 1949 gegründet (The Federal Republic was founded in 1949). Who does something is expressed with "von": Der Bundeskanzler wird vom Bundestag gewählt.

k.b1-3.gr.ex.2.1: The minimum wage applies to everyone who works in Germany.
k.b1-3.gr.ex.3.1: Every employee is entitled to paid holiday.
k.b1-3.gr.rde: Relative clauses describe a noun more precisely. The relative pronoun takes its gender from the noun and its case from the relative clause: der Kollege, der mir hilft (the colleague who helps me) / den ich frage (whom I ask) / dem ich danke (whom I thank). The verb goes at the end.

k.b1-4.gr: Infinitive with zu, um … zu, damit
k.b1-4.gr.ex.0.1: Paper goes in the blue bin.
k.b1-4.gr.ex.1.1: I try to buy less plastic.
k.b1-4.gr.ex.2.1: We air the room briefly to save heating costs.
k.b1-4.gr.ex.3.1: Bottles with a deposit are taken back to the shop.
k.b1-4.gr.rde: Many expressions are followed by zu + infinitive: Es ist wichtig, Müll zu trennen (It is important to sort rubbish). Purpose: um … zu (same subject) – Ich fahre Rad, um Geld zu sparen (I cycle to save money). damit (different subject) – Ich erkläre es, damit meine Kinder es verstehen (I explain it so that my children understand).

k.b1-5.gr.rde: Past perfect = hatte/war + past participle. It describes what had happened before another event in the past: Nachdem die Mauer gefallen war, wurde Deutschland 1990 wiedervereinigt (After the Wall had fallen, Germany was reunified in 1990).
k.b1-6.dia.0.2: Which big cities are there in Saxony?

k.b1-6.gr.ex.2.1: The head of government of Saxony is called Minister-President.
k.b1-6.gr.ex.3.1: Saxon Switzerland lies on the Elbe.
k.b1-6.gr.rde: The genitive shows belonging: die Hauptstadt des Freistaates Sachsen (the capital of the Free State of Saxony), die Farben der Flagge (the colours of the flag). Articles: des (masc./neut., noun + -s/-es), der (fem./plural). In written German the genitive often follows wegen, während, trotz.

k.b1-7.gr.rde: In the DTZ you write a letter/email with four guiding points in about 30 minutes. Cover ALL four points with 1–2 sentences each. Structure: place/date, subject line, greeting, introduction (reason), four points, closing (request for a reply), sign-off, name. Link sentences with: deshalb (therefore), außerdem (also), trotzdem (nevertheless), leider (unfortunately), zuerst, dann, zum Schluss.

k.b1-8.gr: Useful phrases for the oral exam
k.b1-8.gr.ex.0.1: In the picture I can see a family having breakfast.
k.b1-8.gr.ex.1.1: In the foreground / in the background …
k.b1-8.gr.ex.2.1: Where I come from in Ukraine it was different: …
k.b1-8.gr.ex.3.1: How about having the party on Saturday?
k.b1-8.gr.rde: The oral DTZ has three parts: 1. Talking about yourself (name, origin, family, work, learning German). 2. Describing a picture and talking about your own experience. 3. Planning something together with a partner (e.g. a party). Phrases for planning: Was hältst du davon, wenn …? (What do you think about …?) Wie wäre es mit …? (How about …?) Ich schlage vor, dass … (I suggest that …) Einverstanden! (Agreed!)
k.b1-8.vok.2.1: on the left / on the right / in the middle
k.b1-9: Listening and reading: announcements, adverts, official notices

k.b1-9.dia.3.2: The payslips. They are listed in the enclosure.

k.b1-9.gr.ex.3.1: You can lodge an objection against this decision within one month.
k.b1-9.gr.rde: First read the task, then the text. Underline key words (when? where? how much?). Watch out for negation (nicht, kein, ohne) and changes ("statt" – instead of, "verschoben" – postponed, "fällt aus" – cancelled). Announcements mention platform, time and delay.

q.SN4: From what age may you vote in local elections (Kommunalwahl) in Saxony (Sachsen)?
q.SN4.e.1: In Saxony you may vote in local elections from 18 (in some other states from 16).
q.SN5: What are the colours of the state flag of Saxony (Sachsen)?
q.SN5.e.1: The state flag of Saxony is white and green.
q.SN6: Where can you find information about political topics in Saxony (Sachsen)?
q.SN6.e.1: The Saxon State Agency for Civic Education provides neutral information about politics free of charge.

q.SN6.ruo.1: at the municipal public order office (Ordnungsamt)

q.SN8.e.1: Saxony is number 4: the state in the far east, on the border with Poland and the Czech Republic.
q.SN9: What is the head of government in Saxony (Sachsen) called?
q.SN9.e.1: The head of government in Saxony is the Minister-President.
q.g1: In Germany, people may openly speak out against the government because …

q.g1.ruo.2: people have the right to vote.

q.g100.e.1: Life insurance is private and voluntary, not statutory social insurance.

q.g101.e.1: Trade unions represent the interests of employees, e.g. on wages and working hours.

q.g102.e.1: The Federal Cross of Merit is Germany's highest award for special services.
q.g102.ruo.3: the honorary title "Hero of the German Democratic Republic"
q.g103: What is called a "traffic light coalition" (Ampelkoalition) in Germany? The cooperation …
q.g103.e.1: "Traffic light" after the party colours: red (SPD), yellow (FDP), green (Greens). It governed from 2021 to 2024.

q.g299.e.1: The recruited workers were called guest workers because people thought they would only stay for a short time.

q.g3.e.1: Under the rule of law, laws apply to everyone – including the state itself. Nobody is above the law.
q.g3.ruo.0: All residents and the state must obey the laws.
q.g3.ruo.1: The state does not have to obey the laws.
q.g3.ruo.2: Only Germans have to obey the laws.
q.g30: Which is not a feature of our democracy?
q.g30.e.1: Press censorship contradicts democracy. The press in Germany is free (Art. 5).
q.g300: From which country did the first guest workers (Gastarbeiter) come to the Federal Republic of Germany?
q.g300.e.1: The Federal Republic signed its first recruitment agreement with Italy in 1955.
q.g31: In Germany, cooperation between parties to form a government is called …
q.g31.e.1: If no party has a majority on its own, several parties form a coalition together.
q.g32: Which is not a branch of state power in Germany?
q.g32.e.1: The three branches of state power are the legislature, the executive and the judiciary. The press is free and does not belong to the state.
q.g33: Which statement is correct? In Germany …
q.g33.e.1: State and religion are separate. There is no state church; the state is religiously neutral.
q.g33.ruo.0: the state and religious communities are separate from each other.
q.g33.ruo.1: the religious communities form the state.
q.g33.ruo.2: the state depends on the religious communities.
q.g33.ruo.3: the state and religious communities form a unit.
q.g34.e.1: Germany is not a monarchy but a republic – there has been no emperor since 1918.
q.g34.ruo.1: a state governed by the rule of law (Rechtsstaat)
q.g35: How does the German state finance social insurance?
q.g35.e.1: Social insurance is financed mainly from social security contributions paid by employees and employers.
q.g36: Which measure provides social security in Germany?
q.g36.e.1: Health insurance protects you when you are ill – it is part of social security.
q.g37: What are the heads of government of most German federal states called?
q.g37.e.1: In most states the head of government is called Minister-President (in Saxony too). In Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen the title is Mayor.
q.g38: The Federal Republic of Germany is a democratic and social …
q.g38.e.1: Art. 20 of the Basic Law: a democratic and social federal state.
q.g39: What does every German federal state have?
q.g39.e.1: Every federal state has its own government and its own parliament (Landtag).
q.g4: Which right is one of the fundamental rights (Grundrechte) in Germany?
q.g4.e.1: Freedom of expression is a fundamental right in the Basic Law (Art. 5). The other answers are not guaranteed fundamental rights.
q.g40: What are the first words of the German national anthem?
q.g40.e.1: The national anthem is the third verse of the "Song of the Germans" and begins with "Unity and justice and freedom".
q.g40.ruo.2: Joy, beautiful spark of the gods …
q.g41: Why is there more than one party in a democracy?
q.g41.e.1: Several parties represent different opinions. Voters can choose between alternatives.
q.g41.ruo.0: because this means the different opinions of citizens are represented
q.g41.ruo.1: so that bribery in politics is limited
q.g42: Who passes a new law in Germany?
q.g42.e.1: Laws are passed by parliament – at federal level by the Bundestag (with the participation of the Bundesrat).
q.g43: When can a party be banned in Germany?
q.g43.e.1: A party can be banned if it fights against the free democratic basic order. The Federal Constitutional Court decides.
q.g43.ruo.0: if its election campaign is too expensive
q.g43.ruo.1: if it fights against the constitution
q.g43.ruo.2: if it criticises the head of state
q.g43.ruo.3: if its programme proposes a new direction
q.g44: Who can citizens in Germany not elect directly?
q.g44.e.1: The Federal President is elected by the Federal Convention, not directly by the people.
q.g45: Which type of insurance does long-term care insurance (Pflegeversicherung) belong to?
q.g45.e.1: Long-term care insurance is part of social insurance – like health, pension, unemployment and accident insurance.
q.g46: The German state has many tasks. Which task is one of them?
q.g46.e.1: The state builds and maintains infrastructure such as roads and schools – paid for from taxes.
q.g46.ruo.2: It supplies all residents with free newspapers.
q.g47: The German state has many tasks. Which task is not one of them?
q.g47.e.1: Everyone pays for their own holidays. That is not a task of the state.
q.g47.ruo.0: It pays for all citizens' holidays.
q.g48: Which body is not one of Germany's constitutional bodies (Verfassungsorgane)?
q.g48.e.1: Constitutional bodies include the Bundestag, Bundesrat, Federal Government, Federal President and Federal Constitutional Court. A "citizens' assembly" is not one of them.
q.g49: Who decides school policy in Germany?
q.g49.e.1: School policy is a matter for the states (cultural sovereignty of the Länder). That is why every federal state has its own school rules.
q.g5: Elections in Germany are free. What does that mean?
q.g5.e.1: Free elections mean: nobody may influence or force you, and your vote must not cause you any disadvantage.
q.g5.ruo.0: You may accept money if you vote for a particular candidate in return.
q.g5.ruo.1: Only people who have never been in prison may vote.
q.g5.ruo.2: Voters may not be influenced or forced to vote in a particular way, and voting must not cause them any disadvantage.
q.g5.ruo.3: Everyone entitled to vote must vote.
q.g50: The economic system in Germany is called …
q.g50.e.1: Social market economy: a free market, but the state ensures social balance and protection.
q.g51: A democratic state under the rule of law (Rechtsstaat) does not include that …
q.g51.e.1: Only the state may arrest people, in accordance with the law – never a private police force for no reason.
q.g51.ruo.0: people can express criticism of the government.
q.g51.ruo.2: people are arrested by a private police force for no reason.
q.g51.ruo.3: someone commits a crime and is arrested for it.
q.g52: What does "sovereignty of the people" (Volkssouveränität) mean? All state authority comes from the ...
q.g52.e.1: Art. 20: "All state authority comes from the people." The people vote and so decide on politics.
q.g53: What does "rule of law" (Rechtsstaat) mean in Germany?
q.g53.e.1: Under the rule of law, the state itself is bound by the law. Citizens can defend themselves against the state in court.
q.g53.ruo.3: The state must obey the laws.
q.g54: Which is not a branch of state power in Germany?
q.g54.e.1: The branches of state power are the legislature, the executive and the judiciary. "Directive" is not a branch of state power.
q.g55.e.1: The picture shows the Reichstag building in Berlin with its glass dome – this is where the Bundestag meets.
q.g55.ruo.0: the seat of the Bundestag in Berlin
q.g55.ruo.1: the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) in Karlsruhe
q.g56: Which office in Germany is part of the municipal administration (Gemeindeverwaltung)?
q.g56.e.1: The public order office (Ordnungsamt) is a municipal office, e.g. for public order and trade.
q.g57: Who is usually elected President of the German Bundestag?
q.g57.e.1: By tradition, the largest parliamentary group provides the President of the Bundestag.
q.g57.ruo.1: the Minister-President (Ministerpräsident) of the largest federal state
q.g57.ruo.3: a member of the largest parliamentary group (Fraktion)
q.g58: Who appoints the ministers of the federal government in Germany?
q.g58.e.1: The ministers are appointed by the Federal President – on the proposal of the Federal Chancellor.
q.g58.ruo.0: the President of the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht)
q.g59: How many years ago was there a Jewish community in what is now Germany for the first time?
q.g59.e.1: The first Jewish community is documented in Cologne in the year 321 – about 1700 years ago.
q.g6: What is the German constitution called?
q.g6.e.1: The German constitution is called the Basic Law (Grundgesetz). It has been in force since 23 May 1949.
q.g60: In Germany, the Bundestag and the Bundesrat belong to the …
q.g60.e.1: The Bundestag and Bundesrat make the laws. That is why they belong to the legislature (law-making power).
q.g61: What does "sovereignty of the people" (Volkssouveränität) mean?
q.g61.e.1: Sovereignty of the people: power in the state comes from the people – they elect the parliaments.
q.g61.ruo.0: The queen/king rules over the people.
q.g61.ruo.1: The Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) is above the constitution.
q.g61.ruo.2: Interest groups exercise sovereignty together with the government.
q.g61.ruo.3: State authority comes from the people.
q.g62: When the parliament of a German federal state is elected, this is called …
q.g62.e.1: The election of a state parliament is called a Landtag election. In Saxony it takes place every five years.
q.g63: What is not part of the executive (Exekutive) in Germany?
q.g63.e.1: Courts belong to the judiciary, not to the executive (government and administration).
q.g64: Today the Federal Republic of Germany is divided into …
q.g64.e.1: Germany is divided into the federation, the federal states and municipalities (municipalities, towns, districts).
q.g64.ruo.1: an eastern state and a western state.
q.g64.ruo.3: the federation (Bund), federal states (Länder) and municipalities (Kommunen).
q.g65: It is not one of the tasks of the German Bundestag …
q.g65.e.1: The federal cabinet is formed by the Federal Chancellor. The Bundestag elects the chancellor, makes laws and scrutinises the government.
q.g66: Which cities have the largest Jewish communities in Germany?
q.g66.e.1: The largest Jewish communities are in Berlin and Munich.
q.g67: What is mainly a task of the federal states in Germany?
q.g67.e.1: School policy is mainly a task of the federal states.
q.g68: Why does the state control the school system in Germany?
q.g68.e.1: Art. 7 of the Basic Law: the entire school system is under the supervision of the state.
q.g68.ruo.0: because there are only state schools in Germany
q.g68.ruo.1: because all pupils must have a school-leaving certificate
q.g68.ruo.2: because there are different schools in the federal states
q.g68.ruo.3: because it is its task under the Basic Law (Grundgesetz)
q.g69: The Federal Republic of Germany has a three-tier administrative structure. What is the lowest political level called?
q.g69.e.1: The lowest level is the municipalities (Kommunen). Above them are the federal states and the federation.
q.g7: Which right is one of the fundamental rights (Grundrechte) guaranteed by the German constitution? The right to …
q.g7.e.1: Art. 4 of the Basic Law guarantees freedom of belief and conscience: everyone may freely choose their religion or world view – or have none.
q.g70: In 1974, German Federal President (Bundespräsident) Gustav Heinemann hands Helmut Schmidt his certificate of appointment as German Federal Chancellor (Bundeskanzler). Which of these is one of the tasks of the German Federal President?
q.g70.e.1: The Federal President proposes a candidate for chancellor to the Bundestag and appoints that person after the election.
q.g70.ruo.0: She/He conducts the business of government.
q.g70.ruo.3: She/He proposes the chancellor (Kanzler) for election.
q.g71: Where does the German Federal Chancellor (Bundeskanzler) spend most time? Most of the time she/he is …
q.g71.e.1: The Chancellery and the Bundestag are in Berlin, so the chancellor mostly works there.
q.g71.ruo.0: in Bonn, because the Federal Chancellery (Bundeskanzleramt) and the Bundestag are there.
q.g71.ruo.1: at Meseberg Palace (Schloss Meseberg), the federal government's guest house, to receive state guests.
q.g71.ruo.2: at Bellevue Palace (Schloss Bellevue), the official residence of the Federal President (Bundespräsident), to receive state guests.
q.g71.ruo.3: in Berlin, because the Federal Chancellery (Bundeskanzleramt) and the Bundestag are there.
q.g72: What is the name of the current Federal Chancellor (Bundeskanzler) of Germany?
q.g72.e.1: Friedrich Merz (CDU) has been Federal Chancellor since May 2025. Note: this answer may change after elections.
q.g73: The two largest parliamentary groups (Fraktionen) in the German Bundestag are currently …
q.g73.e.1: After the 2025 federal election, CDU/CSU and AfD are the two largest parliamentary groups. The answer depends on the current election result.
q.g74: What is the parliament for the whole of Germany called?
q.g74.e.1: The parliament for the whole of Germany is the Bundestag. The federal states have Landtage.
q.g75: What is the name of Germany's current head of state?
q.g75.e.1: The head of state is the Federal President, currently Frank-Walter Steinmeier. This may change after the next election.
q.g76: What does the abbreviation CDU stand for in Germany?
q.g76.e.1: CDU = Christian Democratic Union of Germany.
q.g77.e.1: The Bundeswehr is the army of the Federal Republic of Germany.
q.g78: What does the abbreviation SPD stand for?
q.g78.e.1: SPD = Social Democratic Party of Germany, the oldest party in Germany (founded 1863/1875).
q.g79: What does the abbreviation FDP stand for in Germany?
q.g8: What is not in the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) of Germany?
q.g8.e.1: The Basic Law guarantees equal rights, but not equal income or wealth for everyone.
q.g8.ruo.1: Everyone should have the same amount of money.
q.g8.ruo.2: Everyone may say what they think.
q.g8.ruo.3: Everyone is equal before the law.
q.g80: Which court in Germany is responsible for interpreting the Basic Law (Grundgesetz)?
q.g80.e.1: The Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe interprets the Basic Law and checks whether laws are constitutional.
q.g81: Who elects the Federal Chancellor (Bundeskanzler) in Germany?
q.g81.e.1: The Federal Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag – on the proposal of the Federal President.
q.g82: Who heads the German federal cabinet (Bundeskabinett)?
q.g82.e.1: The federal cabinet consists of the chancellor and the ministers. The chancellor heads it and sets the guidelines of policy.
q.g83: Who elects the German Federal Chancellor (Bundeskanzler)?
q.g83.e.1: The Bundestag elects the chancellor, not the people directly.
q.g84: What is the main task of the German Federal President (Bundespräsident)? She/He …
q.g84.e.1: The Federal President represents Germany at home and abroad. Policy is made by the government.
q.g85: Who makes up the German Bundesrat?
q.g85.e.1: The Bundesrat is made up of members of the state governments. This is how the federal states take part in federal politics.
q.g85.ruo.1: the ministers of the federal government
q.g85.ruo.2: the government representatives of the federal states
q.g86: Who elects the Federal President (Bundespräsident) in Germany?
q.g86.e.1: The Federal Convention elects the Federal President. It consists of the members of the Bundestag and an equal number of representatives of the federal states.
q.g87: Who is the head of state of the Federal Republic of Germany?
q.g87.e.1: The head of state is the Federal President. The head of government is the Federal Chancellor.
q.g88: The parliamentary opposition in the German Bundestag …
q.g88.e.1: The opposition scrutinises and criticises the government and offers alternatives.
q.g88.ruo.1: decides who becomes a federal minister.
q.g88.ruo.2: decides who sits in the Bundesrat.
q.g88.ruo.3: proposes the heads of government of the federal states.
q.g89: In Germany, what is the group of members of one party in parliament called?
q.g89.e.1: The members of one party in parliament form a parliamentary group (Fraktion).
q.g9: Which fundamental right (Grundrecht) in Germany applies only to foreigners? The fundamental right to …
q.g9.e.1: Only people without German citizenship who are politically persecuted can apply for asylum (Art. 16a).
q.g90: The German federal states take part in federal legislation through …
q.g90.e.1: The federal states take part in federal laws through the Bundesrat; some laws require its consent.
q.g91: In Germany, a change of government in a federal state can affect federal politics. Governing becomes …
q.g91.e.1: If a state government changes, the majority in the Bundesrat can change. Then it becomes harder to get laws passed.
q.g91.ruo.0: more difficult if the majority in the Bundestag changes as a result.
q.g91.ruo.1: easier if new parties enter the Bundesrat as a result.
q.g91.ruo.2: more difficult if the majority in the Bundesrat changes as a result.
q.g91.ruo.3: easier if it is a wealthy federal state.
q.g92: What does the abbreviation CSU stand for in Germany?
q.g92.e.1: CSU = Christian Social Union. It only stands for election in Bavaria and forms a joint parliamentary group with the CDU.
q.g93: The more "second votes" (Zweitstimmen) a party receives in a federal election (Bundestagswahl), the …
q.g93.e.1: The second vote decides how seats are distributed: more second votes, more seats.
q.g93.ruo.0: fewer first votes (Erststimmen) it can have.
q.g93.ruo.1: more of the party's constituency candidates (Direktkandidaten) enter parliament.
q.g93.ruo.2: greater the risk of having to form a coalition.
q.g93.ruo.3: more seats the party gets in parliament.
q.g94: From what age may you vote in elections to the German Bundestag?
q.g94.e.1: You may vote in the federal election from the age of 18.
q.g95: What applies to most children in Germany?
q.g95.e.1: Schooling is compulsory in Germany. Children must go to school – home schooling is generally not allowed.
q.g96: How can someone who denies the Holocaust be punished?
q.g96.e.1: Holocaust denial is incitement to hatred (§ 130 of the Criminal Code): up to five years in prison or a fine.
q.g96.ruo.1: up to 100 hours of community service
q.g96.ruo.2: not at all, Holocaust denial is allowed
q.g96.ruo.3: with imprisonment of up to five years or a fine
q.g97: What do you automatically pay in Germany if you are in permanent employment?
q.g97.e.1: In permanent employment, social insurance contributions are deducted automatically from your wages.
q.g98: If members of the German Bundestag change their parliamentary group (Fraktion), …
q.g98.e.1: If members change parliamentary group, the governing coalition may lose its majority in the Bundestag.
q.g98.ruo.0: they may no longer attend sessions of parliament.
q.g98.ruo.1: the government may lose its majority.
q.g98.ruo.2: the Federal President (Bundespräsident) must give consent beforehand.
q.g98.ruo.3: the voters of these members may vote again.
q.g99: Who pays for social insurance in Germany?
q.g99.e.1: Employers and employees usually each pay half of the social insurance contributions.
